newsitem.title: USA: Ana, Fabian and Mindy on hurricane name list.
newsitem.headline: Ana, Fabian and Mindy on hurricane name list.

text.p: If a hurricane called Wanda hits the Caribbean and Atlantic this storm season, few people are likely to be laughing.
Wanda would be the 21st hurricane or tropical storm of the season, according to a list of names drawn up by forecasters at the National Hurricane Centre.
In 1996 they got as far as Marco as 13 storms ripped through the region. This year's first has been christened Ana.

That would be followed by Bill, Claudette, Danny, Erika, Fabian, Grace, Henri, Isabel, Juan, Kate, Larry, Mindy, Nicholas, Odette, Peter, Rose, Sam, Teresa, Victor and Wanda during the season that begins June 1 and ends Nov. 30.

The letters Q, U, X, Y and Z are never used. If a season is so busy the list of names is exhausted, the Centre would move to a backup plan of naming storms after the letters of the Greek alphabet. That possibility loomed in 1995, the busiest season since the birth of the alphabetized name list, when the season consumed 19 of the 21 names before fizzling out.

Hurricanes in the West Indies have had informal names for centuries, as many of the worst were named after the saint's day on which they occurred. For example, Hurricane San Felipe (the first) hit Puerto Rico on Sept. 13, 1876, and Hurricane San Felipe (the second) and hit Puerto Rico on Sept. 13, 1928.

The United States adopted its first organised storm naming system in 1950, for three years naming storms after the military's phonetic alphabet -- Abel, Baker, Charlie, etc. In 1953 the U.S. Weather Service began using women's names for storms, a process that became more politically correct in 1979, when men's names were added to the list for storms in the Atlantic, Caribbean and Gulf of Mexico.
It is hard to imagine a Hurricane Fifi, but she caused one of the western hemisphere's worst natural disasters in 1974 with floods that left an estimated 5,000 people dead in Central America.

But forecasters said they try to pick short, easily remembered names that reflect naming-practices in the cultures of the French, English, Spanish and Creole-speaking places hurricanes most-often hit.

The U.S. National Weather Service's National Hurricane Centre assigns a name to a storm when sustained winds reach tropical storm strength of 39 mph (63 kph). The centre keeps six annual lists of names, used in turn, but retires the name of the biggest storms to minimise confusion later.
For example there will never be another Hurricane Andrew, the monster storm of 1992 that devastated Florida and also caused heavy damage in Louisiana.
Names for the lists are selected from library sources and agreed upon by nations involved during international meetings of the World Meteorological Organisation.
